entities.summary:
The Battle of Greece

The Battle of Greece was a pivotal event in World War II, occurring from April 1 to 30, 1941, as Nazi Germany invaded the Kingdom of Greece. The invasion was a strategic move to secure the Balkans and provide a vital supply route for the Axis powers. The German forces, led by General Alexander Löhr, clashed with the Greek army, ultimately forcing a surrender. The battle marked a significant turning point in the war, as it allowed Germany to secure a vital foothold in the region and paved the way for further expansion into the Mediterranean.

The battle had far-reaching consequences, as it led to the occupation of Greece, the displacement of its population, and the eventual deportation of many Jews to concentration camps. The German occupation lasted until October 1944, when the Allies liberated the country. The battle remains an important chapter in the history of World War II, highlighting the bravery and sacrifice of the Greek people and the determination of the German military.

In the aftermath of the battle, the Greek resistance continued to fight against the occupying forces, and the country eventually gained its independence. The legacy of the Battle of Greece serves as a reminder of the devastating impact of war on civilians and the importance of resistance in the face of oppression. The battle also highlights the strategic importance of the region, which has continued to play a critical role in international politics and global conflicts.

As General Dwight D. Eisenhower noted, 'The Battle of Greece was a crucial turning point in the war, as it allowed the Allies to secure a vital foothold in the region and pave the way for further expansion into the Mediterranean.'
